description_en: Marcus Junius Brutus was born around 85 BCE to Marcus Junius Brutus the Elder and Servilia, who later became Julius Caesar's mistress.
Brutus was adopted by his uncle Quintus Servilius Caepio and took the name Quintus Caepio Brutus.
Brutus was a follower of Stoic philosophy and an admirer of his uncle Cato the Younger.
Brutus opposed Pompey initially (over his father's death) but joined Pompey's side against Caesar in the civil war.
After Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus, Caesar pardoned Brutus and appointed him governor of Cisalpine Gaul.
Brutus served as urban praetor in 44 BCE.
Brutus was a principal leader in the conspiracy that assassinated Julius Caesar on March 15, 44 BCE.
After Caesar's assassination, Brutus fled to Athens and then to the eastern provinces, where he and Cassius raised armies.
Brutus and Cassius were defeated by Mark Antony and Octavian at the two battles of Philippi in October 42 BCE.
Brutus committed suicide after his defeat at Philippi.
Brutus was married to Porcia, daughter of Cato the Younger.
Brutus was a respected orator and wrote philosophical works, all of which are now lost.
The rumor that Brutus was Caesar's natural son, based on Caesar's long affair with Servilia, circulated in antiquity but is unverifiable.
Brutus issued coins (the famous 'Eid Mar' denarius) commemorating Caesar's assassination with daggers and a liberty cap.
Cicero dedicated several philosophical works to Brutus and maintained a correspondence with him.
Shakespeare's 'Et tu, Brute?' and depiction of Brutus as a tragic hero are literary inventions, not historically attested words.
